sections.title: A dataset is a stack of flash cards
paragraphs: Think of a {{dataset}} as a whole deck of flash cards, not a single card. One card is an example: an {{input}} on the front and a {{target}} on the back. The deck is every card you are willing to teach from.

In {{supervisedLearning}}, that deck is what the {{model}} studies. Each row pairs something you show the {{model}} with the answer you want it to learn. Without a full set of pairs, there is nothing to practice on.

A {{dataset}} can be tiny or huge. The four XOR {{input}} pairs — (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), and (1,1) — form a {{dataset}}. Ten thousand labeled emails form a {{dataset}}. The shape stays the same: rows of {{labeledData}}.
People sometimes say "data" when they mean raw files with no answers. That pile is not yet a supervised {{dataset}}. You still need agreed {{target}}s before training can start.
When the Neural network lab asks you to pick a {{dataset}}, it is offering different decks of cards — same idea as flash cards, different puzzles on each card.
bullets: {{dataset}} — the full collection of training rows.
Each row — one {{input}} paired with one {{target}}.
Raw files alone — not a supervised {{dataset}} until labeled.

check.prompt: A teammate dumps 20,000 untagged support tickets into a folder and calls it "our training {{dataset}}." What is missing?
choices: A second copy of the same folder
check.explanation: A supervised {{dataset}} needs {{labeledData}}. Tickets without {{target}}s are only {{input}}s — the {{model}} has nothing to grade {{prediction}}s against.

aside.title: See datasets in the lab
aside.body: The Neural network lab lets you switch between built-in puzzles and your own rows — each choice is a different {{dataset}}.

sections.title: Same shape, different puzzles
paragraphs: Every built-in {{dataset}} in the lab uses the same row shape: two numbers as the {{input}}, and a {{target}} the {{model}} should predict. Plot those two numbers as a point on a graph and the four pairs (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), and (1,1) sit at the corners of a square — so people call each pair a corner.
AND is the easy deck. Only the corner (1,1) maps to {{target}} 1; the other three corners map to 0. A simple straight boundary can separate the answers.

XOR is the classic hard deck. Corners where the inputs differ — (0,1) and (1,0) — map to 1; matching corners (0,0) and (1,1) map to 0. No single straight line separates them, so a tiny network usually needs a hidden layer.
The 3-class deck teaches a different kind of {{target}}: pick one class among three instead of a yes/no style answer. Softmax output fits that multi-class setup.
Click each puzzle below. Notice the {{input}} corners look similar while the {{target}} pattern — and the teaching point — changes.

reveals.prompt: AND dataset — when is the target 1?
reveals.reveal: Only at corner (1,1), when both inputs are 1. One straight boundary can separate the answers, so AND is easier to learn than XOR.

reveals.prompt: XOR dataset — when is the target 1?
reveals.reveal: At corners (0,1) and (1,0), when the two inputs differ. Matching corners (0,0) and (1,1) are 0. This pattern usually needs a hidden layer.
A class label among three options (0, 1, or 2). Softmax splits probability across three outputs instead of a single yes/no score.

check.prompt: You want learners to see why a hidden layer matters. Which lab {{dataset}} makes that point clearest?
check.answer: XOR — input pairs that need a non-linear split
choices: XOR — input pairs that need a non-linear split
A single training row with no target
check.explanation: XOR is not linearly separable: the four corners cannot be split with one straight line. AND can, so it is a weaker demo of why hidden layers help.

sections.title: Custom rows and what comes next
paragraphs: Custom mode lets you invent your own {{dataset}}: type {{input}} numbers and {{target}}s, then train on those rows. You are building the flash-card deck yourself.
Keep the same discipline as any supervised set. Every row needs a clear {{target}}. Mix-ups — wrong labels, missing answers, or inconsistent rules — teach the {{model}} the wrong lesson.
Teaching shortcut in the Neural network lab: it often trains on every row you provide. That is fine for learning how training feels, but real projects do not stop there.
Next lesson — **Train vs test** — explains why we hold some rows out of the {{dataset}} as a {{testSet}} so we can measure {{generalization}} honestly.
After that, the **Neural network lab** is where you pick AND, XOR, 3-class, or custom and watch a tiny {{model}} learn from the deck you chose.
bullets: Honest labels — bad {{target}}s train the wrong pattern.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: what is a supervised {{dataset}} made of?
check.explanation: A {{dataset}} is not "some files somewhere." It is a collection of {{labeledData}} — each row pairs an {{input}} with a {{target}} the {{model}} should learn.

recapQuestions.answer: Four XOR input pairs with known 0/1 targets
choices: Four XOR input pairs with known 0/1 targets
A zip file of photos with no tags
Server logs with no agreed labels
recapQuestions.explanation: The four XOR corners — (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) — with {{target}}s are {{labeledData}}. Files without labels are not yet a supervised {{dataset}}, no matter how you name the folder.

recapQuestions.prompt: Why does the lab offer both AND and XOR {{dataset}}s?
recapQuestions.answer: Same row shape, different difficulty and teaching points
choices: Same row shape, different difficulty and teaching points
AND and XOR use completely different column formats
AND cannot be stored as rows
recapQuestions.explanation: Both puzzles use input–target rows. AND is easier (linearly separable); XOR shows when a hidden layer helps. Different decks, same idea of a {{dataset}}.
